<reason>PRO built and held a clear decision rule—asymmetric, irreversible error plus information asymmetry—and defended it under pressure with concrete, plausible rebuttal structures (non-controlling stakes, host-law trustees, divest-on-trigger) that substantially neutralized CON's "ban in a wig" line. CON's best material was the midstream/host-license point and the capital-starvation objection, and A4.4's financing-vs-flow distinction was a genuinely good answer to PRO's fork, as was A4.7 on jurisdiction over listed bids. But CON never engaged the Japan/Lynas reversibility example, and its central claim that a presumption deters greenfield operators stayed asserted rather than shown. PRO's closing correctly noted CON had conceded most components of the mechanism, leaving the dispute to who proposes mitigation first—a narrow change that CON's "missing mine" warning did not clearly outweigh. PRO's clipped Rebuttal 1 was a real but minor execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B4.4/B4.6–4.7 answer to CON's pressure question: the Lynas-style "stalled deposit can be financed later" reply to reversibility, paired with the fork "if title is irrelevant the block costs nothing; if losing the bidder kills the mine, title is a supply lever." CON's A4.4 response (title decides financing, not licensed flow) was a coherent counter, but CON left the reversibility example unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
